h1: How a new beer goes from idea to shelf, for cross-functional teams
title: How a New Beer Goes From Idea to Shelf | Craft Beer School
desc: The stages a new beer passes through, from concept and pilot brews to costing, excise label approval and launch, for cross-functional teams.
teaser: Brewing the beer is often the quickest part. Label approvals, packaging and costings take longer than most marketing plans allow.
standfirst: Launching a new beer involves marketing, brewing, quality, procurement, finance, regulatory and sales. Each sees a different part of the process. Here is the whole journey in order, so cross-functional teams can plan together.
sections: Stage one: the idea and the brief

Most new beers start with a commercial question. Is there a gap in the portfolio? Do consumers want something lighter, stronger, wheat-based or lower in alcohol? Is a competitor gaining in a segment? The answer becomes a brief: the target drinker, the occasion, the price point, the pack and the states where it will sell.

A good brief also says what the beer should taste like in plain words. "Crisp, light, slightly sweet, low bitterness" gives brewers something to work with. "Premium and exciting" does not. Our guide to the beer brand portfolio explains how a new beer should fit alongside existing brands.
Stage two: recipe and pilot brews

Brewers turn the brief into a recipe: malt bill, any adjuncts such as rice or maize, hops, yeast, alcohol target and process. They brew small pilot batches, often several versions, then run tasting panels to compare them with the brief and with competitor beers.

A pilot brew might take two to four weeks from brew day to drinkable beer, longer for lagers. Each round of changes adds time. Teams that agree tasting criteria early save rounds.

Brewers also check that the recipe suits the plant. A beer that needs a long cold conditioning period ties up tanks that existing brands depend on. A recipe built around a hop variety that is hard to import may be beautiful in the pilot and impossible to supply at volume. These practical questions belong in the pilot stage, not after the brand name is chosen.
Stage three: consumer and sensory testing

Shortlisted recipes may go to consumer tests, where target drinkers taste and rate them. They may also go to trained sensory panels, which describe them precisely. Tastings within a company should always be optional, in small measured samples, with spit cups and non-drinkers welcome.

This stage often reveals a gap between what marketing described and what drinkers prefer. It is cheaper to learn that now than after launch.
Stage four: scale-up, costing and supply

A recipe that works in a pilot plant has to work in the main brewhouse, with its own vessel shapes, hop utilisation and fermentation behaviour. Brewers run a scale-up trial and adjust. Procurement checks that every ingredient and packaging material can be sourced reliably. Finance builds the cost per hectolitre and the margin on net sales after excise.

Shelf life testing starts here too. The beer must hold its flavour for its intended best before period, including in Indian summer storage conditions.
Stage five: pack, label and approvals

Design develops the label and pack. Regulatory checks it against FSSAI and legal metrology requirements. Then each state's excise department must usually register the label and price before the beer can be sold there. This step varies by state, can be tied to the financial year and often takes longer than any other.

Many launches slip here. A label printed before approval, or a change requested by one state, can delay the whole plan. Build the approval calendar into the project from day one.
Stage six: production, release and launch

The first production batches follow the agreed recipe and process. Quality checks each batch against the new specification and signs it off for release. Our guide to how a beer batch is released explains those checks. Sales teams need training, tasting notes and answers to the obvious questions before the beer reaches distributors and outlets.

Launch is not the end. Track volumes, depletions, repeat purchase and complaints in the first months. Brewers may fine-tune the recipe within the approved specification. Some beers become flagships. Many are seasonal or limited. Some are withdrawn. Our guide to flagship beer strategy covers how to decide which beers deserve long-term support.

The most common reason for delays is one team not understanding another's constraints: marketing planning a launch date without allowing for lager conditioning time, or brewing finishing a recipe before procurement checks a hop variety's availability. Cross-functional teams that understand the whole journey set realistic dates and hit them.

A simple shared timeline helps: each stage, its owner, its typical duration and the decision that closes it. Put the state approval windows on it first, because they rarely move.
faqs: How long does it take to launch a new beer?
It varies widely. Brewing trials may take weeks, but costing, packaging and state label approvals often take months, so plan the full timeline early.
Who is involved in new beer development?
Marketing, brewing, quality, procurement, finance, regulatory and sales all play a part, from the brief through approvals to launch.
Why do new beer launches get delayed?
State excise label and price approvals, packaging lead times and extra rounds of recipe changes are the most common causes.
